sections.html:
• Name: Tangerine Tiger Shrimp
  • Other names: Tupfel Shrimp
  • Scientific name: Caridina serrata
  • Optimal tank size: 40 litres
  • Breeding: Easy
  • Optimal KH: 0–4
  • Optimal TDS: 100–200
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: Algae eater/omnivore
  • Temperament: Peaceful
  • Colour: semi-transparent with a yellow, blue, purple or greenish tint

Note: the Tangerine Tiger Shrimp is sometimes called 'Neocaridina serrata' for a population from the Lam Tsuen river, in the central New Territories (Hong Kong). This is a mistake: biologists examined these shrimp and concluded they are Caridina cantonensis (Blue bolt shrimp).

Tangerine Tiger shrimp are not very common in the aquarium trade, but they are peaceful, hardy and easy to care for, and suit beginners.

Caridina serrata will crossbreed with most Caridina species (except Amano shrimp), producing new colour patterns or a loss of colour and a return to wild-type coloration. To keep the line, a species tank or a community tank with Neocaridina is ideal; they can be kept with Neocaridina without risk of interbreeding.

Compatible tankmates: other shrimp (cherry, snowball, ghost, Amano, bee shrimp, etc.), freshwater snails (Japanese trapdoor, ramshorn, nerite, Malaysian trumpet snails, etc.), and small peaceful fish (pygmy corydoras, otocinclus).

Avoid: most crayfish and freshwater crabs. Even small African dwarf frogs will try to catch the shrimp.

Caridina serrata was first found and described from Hong Kong Island in 1860. Since then these shrimp have not been found anywhere else. They are endemic to Hong Kong and have a locally confined distribution.

Note: Due to pollution, collection for the aquarium trade and urbanisation of Hong Kong Island, this endemic species is seriously threatened and should be regarded as endangered.
Tangerine Tiger shrimp inhabit small slow-moving streams or rivers, both in the mountains and in the plains.

Given their small size, Tangerine Tiger shrimp do not need a large tank. Ideally a 40-litre tank suits them perfectly. They can live and thrive in smaller tanks, but water parameters then need constant control, because dwarf shrimp prefer consistency and in small tanks everything can go wrong very fast. For beginners, a tank of at least 40 litres is advised.

Most Caridina species are finicky about water parameters, but this is not the case here. They are probably the hardiest Caridina and can handle a wide range of parameters.

  • Temperature: optimal 20–24 °C; they can tolerate lower or higher. Higher temperature increases metabolism and breeding rate but reduces lifespan.
  • pH: slightly acidic to neutral, 6.0–7.5.
  • Hardness: 4–8 GH and 0–4 KH.

Check water parameters and do small water changes. Dwarf shrimp do not like big and sudden changes, which can cause serious moulting problems (like the 'white ring of death').

For ideal conditions, good quality RO/DI water is recommended. It contains no minerals, so all parameters (pH, KH, GH, TDS) must be set manually with shrimp re-mineralisers.

Be careful with copper: crabs, shrimp and crayfish do not tolerate copper-based medications.

Acclimate them carefully and very slowly, as with all invertebrates; 2–3 hours is generally enough.

The most important factor is a stable nitrogen cycle; shrimp are sensitive to ammonia and nitrates.

Active substrate (for example ADA Amazonia aqua soil, Fluval Plant and Shrimp Stratum, Akadama-Bonsai soil) helps if you need to keep pH below 7.0. Without aiming for the best breeding rate, sand or gravel (inert substrate) can also be used.

Sponge or matten filters are recommended for any shrimp tank: cheap, easy to maintain, with plenty of grazing surface and safe for baby shrimp.

Since they live in streams and rivulets, aeration is highly recommended.

Light is not important for the shrimp; adapt it to the plants in the tank.

Decorations are not necessary, but they appreciate leaves, rocks, wood, PVC pipes, etc. as hiding places and as surfaces for algae and biofilm.

Tangerine Tiger shrimp are opportunistic omnivores. They use their specialised chelipeds to consume leaf litter, algae, detritus, etc. As scavengers they are not picky and will eat just about any food they find on the bottom of the tank.

In a well-established tank they can usually find enough food (algae and biofilm) by themselves. To keep them healthy, supplement them from time to time with common shrimp foods. Add some blanched zucchini, cucumber, lettuce, carrots, spinach and leaves; Indian almond leaves are a good choice.

Do not overfeed them: overfeeding fouls the water and can kill shrimp. Feed once a day (or once every 2–3 days in a mature tank), in rations that last up to 3–6 hours. Afterwards, depending on the food, remove uneaten parts to prevent poor water quality and parasite contamination.

Calcium plays a major role in any shrimp's health.

In a planted tank they search through and graze on the plants. They do not eat healthy plants, but will eat dying, rotting or decaying ones.

Tangerine Tiger shrimp are completely harmless and will not bother anybody in a community tank. They are not territorial and prefer to be in large groups.

The bigger the colony, the safer they feel and the more confident they act. This makes them suitable for keeping with other freshwater fish, shrimp or snails.

• Larger shrimp are females; males are smaller.
  • Females' abdomen is wider and curves downward to protect the eggs; males are thinner.
  • Presence of a saddle or eggs; females have longer pleopods to carry eggs.
  • Females usually have the most marked colours compared with males.

Tangerine Tiger shrimp are prolific and breed quickly if water parameters are stable and there is enough food. Caridina serrata is a fully freshwater species with abbreviated larval development lacking planktonic stages. Depending on temperature they become sexually mature in 3–4 months.

In nature breeding is mainly restricted to the wet season, as water temperatures rise at the start of the summer monsoon. In aquariums they can breed all year round.

Females moult before mating and release a chemical substance into the water to attract males, which swim in frenzied circuits seeking her.

Egg number depends on female size, usually 30–40. The female carries the eggs under her tail for the whole incubation (4–5 weeks depending on temperature), fanning them regularly with pleopods.

Young hatch as tiny replicas of the adults, about 2 mm long, completely independent, with the same feeding preferences. Their colour becomes more intense as they mature.

Tangerine Tiger shrimp have a very interesting and attractive colour. Yellow/orange variations are often seen in the trade, but they have many more colour variants. Their translucent bodies can acquire a blue, purple or even greenish tint.

Note: wild-type Caridina serrata are more brown or colourless, which helps them blend into the environment. The fancy colours were bred, and slowly brighter colours appeared until the strains were obtained.

In addition to dark irregular stripes, their bodies are covered with many tiny dots. Caridina serrata also has a very short rostrum compared with other shrimp species.

Like all dwarf shrimp, Caridina serrata usually grows to 2–3 cm. Once a proper aquarium is set up and optimum conditions are met, they can reproduce and live 1.5–2 years.
